title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS TITHE 10%—OR IS THAT AN OLD COVENANT REQUIREMENT?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS TITHE 10%—OR IS THAT AN OLD COVENANT REQUIREMENT?
What if the question God is asking is not, “Did you give Me exactly ten percent?” but something far more uncomfortable: “After everything My Son gave for you… how much of you actually belongs to Me?”
There is a moment that happens in churches almost everywhere.
The sermon ends.
The music softens.
Someone begins talking about giving.
And suddenly, people get uncomfortable.
Some reach for their wallets.
Some reach for their phones.
Some feel grateful.
Some feel guilty.
Some quietly calculate ten percent.
And some sit there wondering something they have been afraid to ask out loud:
“Does God actually require Christians to tithe ten percent?”
Maybe you were taught that if you do not tithe, you are robbing God.
Maybe someone quoted Malachi 3 and told you that financial hardship might be happening because you withheld God’s ten percent.
Maybe you were taught that the first ten percent belongs to your local church and anything beyond that is an offering.
Or perhaps you came from the opposite side.
“Jesus fulfilled the Law. Tithing is Old Testament. Christians are under grace. I can give whatever I want—or nothing at all.”
Both positions can sound biblical when isolated verses are placed behind them.
But Scripture deserves something better than slogans.
And so does your conscience.
Because this question is not ultimately about percentages.
It is about worship.
It is about ownership.
It is about grace.
And before this is finished, the uncomfortable question may no longer be whether God wants ten percent of your money.
The question may become:
What happened to the other ninety percent?
To understand tithing, we first have to understand the word itself.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “tithe” is מַעֲשֵׂר — ma‘aser.
It means a tenth.
That matters because biblical tithing was not originally a vague synonym for “giving money to God.” It referred to something specific within Israel’s covenant life.

Leviticus says that the tithe of the land belonged to the LORD and was holy to Him. Leviticus 27:30 specifically speaks of the produce of the land, while the following verses also address herd and flock.
This was part of Israel’s covenant structure.
It supported worship.
It supported those assigned to sacred service.
It was intertwined with Israel’s agricultural life and covenant obligations.
And yes, the Old Testament takes it seriously.
Then comes the passage almost everyone has heard during a sermon about giving.
Malachi 3:10.
The Hebrew begins:
הָבִיאוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַמַּעֲשֵׂר אֶל־בֵּית הָאוֹצָר
Havi'u et-kol-hamma'aser el-beit ha'otzar.
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse…”
The word הַמַּעֲשֵׂר — hamma‘aser means “the tithe” or “the tenth.”

And God says there should be food in His house. The historical picture is not simply a modern Christian placing ten percent of a salary into an offering envelope. Malachi addresses Israel within its covenant setting, with the tithe being brought into the storehouse and providing food connected with the life of God’s house.
That context matters.
We should never weaken Scripture.
But neither should we move a command from one covenant setting into another without asking how the New Testament handles it.
Someone may immediately object:
“But Abraham tithed before Moses.”
Correct.

Genesis records Abraham giving Melchizedek a tenth after the battle, and Hebrews 7 deliberately remembers that event. The Greek text uses δεκάτην — dekatēn, “a tenth.” Hebrews says Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything to Melchizedek.
That demonstrates something important.
Giving a tenth existed before the Mosaic Law.
But there is a difference between showing that Abraham once gave a tenth and establishing a universal command requiring every Christian to give exactly ten percent of every paycheck.
The text must be allowed to say what it says.
Not less.
Not more.
Then Jesus enters the conversation.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronts the scribes and Pharisees because they meticulously tithed even small herbs while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law”—justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He tells them they should have practiced those things without neglecting the others.
So Jesus certainly did not mock tithing.
He did not praise disobedience.
But notice the setting.
He is speaking before the cross, to people living within Israel’s covenant world, while confronting teachers of the Law about their hypocritical observance of that Law.
And then something happens that changes everything.
The cross.
The resurrection.
The New Covenant.
Jesus does not merely arrive to improve religious bookkeeping.
He gives Himself.
His blood is poured out.
His body is broken.
The sinless One dies for sinners.
The debt we could never pay is answered not by ten percent of Christ…
but by all of Christ.
And when the apostles begin teaching New Covenant churches how to give, something fascinating happens.
They speak about generosity repeatedly.
They speak about supporting ministry.
They speak about helping believers in need.
They speak about sharing materially.
They speak about giving regularly and intentionally.
They speak about generosity so radical that it can hurt.

But in the central New Testament instructions to churches about giving, the emphasis shifts from calculating a mandatory percentage toward willing, purposeful, proportionate, generous giving flowing from grace.
Paul tells the Corinthians:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ
hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia
“Each one as he has purposed in the heart…”
Then come words that should terrify anyone who has ever tried to manipulate Christians into opening their wallets:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs
“not from grief or from necessity/compulsion.”
And then:
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ Θεός
hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos
“For God loves a cheerful giver.”
That is 2 Corinthians 9:7. The Greek text explicitly contrasts giving from the heart with giving under ἀνάγκη — anankē, necessity or compulsion.
Read that again.
God does not need to emotionally extort His children.
Grace does not put a spiritual gun against your conscience.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be manufactured through panic.
And Paul gives another principle in 1 Corinthians 16.
Speaking about a collection for believers, he tells Christians to set something aside regularly, ὅ τι ἂν εὐοδῶται—in keeping with how one is prospering.
That sounds less like careless spontaneity and more like intentional generosity.
Regular.
Thoughtful.
Proportionate.
Purposeful.
So does that mean Christians should never give ten percent?
Not at all.
Ten percent can be an excellent discipline.
For some believers, it may be a helpful starting point.
For someone learning to put God ahead of consumption, deliberately setting aside ten percent may train the heart away from greed.
But we should be careful about calling a useful benchmark a universal New Covenant command when the apostolic instructions themselves do not impose that percentage on the churches.
And here is where grace becomes far more challenging than a calculator.
Because legalism asks:
“What is the minimum I have to give?”
Grace asks:
“How can everything God has entrusted to me serve Christ?”
That is a much more dangerous question.
Ten percent can actually become comfortable.
Imagine earning $100.
“Ten belongs to God.”
Then what?
Does the remaining $90 belong entirely to you?
Imagine earning $10,000.
“One thousand for God.”
And the other $9,000?
Is Jesus Lord of that too?
This is where the Gospel destroys our little accounting system.
Because the Christian does not belong ten percent to Jesus.
The Christian belongs to Jesus.
Your money belongs to Jesus.
Your house belongs to Jesus.
Your career belongs to Jesus.
Your business belongs to Jesus.
Your talents belong to Jesus.
Your Saturday belongs to Jesus.
Your retirement belongs to Jesus.
Your influence belongs to Jesus.
Your phone belongs to Jesus.
Your plans belong to Jesus.
Even the breath currently moving through your lungs is mercy.
Christian stewardship begins when we stop asking how little we can surrender while still considering ourselves obedient.
And this is where the story gets painfully personal.
Because some people give ten percent faithfully…
and still worship money.
They tithe while ignoring a struggling family member.
They tithe while exploiting employees.
They tithe while drowning themselves in luxury.
They tithe while refusing generosity unless there is a tax deduction, recognition, applause, or promised blessing attached.
Jesus confronted precisely that kind of religious mathematics when He rebuked people who carefully counted herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
You can calculate ten percent perfectly…
and still withhold your heart.
But the opposite error is just as dangerous.
Some Christians hear “we are not under the Old Covenant tithe” and quietly translate that into:
“Wonderful. I don't have to give.”
But if grace makes us less generous than people living under the Law, perhaps we have misunderstood grace.
Look at Jesus.
He did not ask what percentage of Himself He was required to surrender.
He gave Himself.
This is the heartbeat beneath Christian generosity.
Paul's appeal to generosity in 2 Corinthians does not end with money.
It rises until it reaches worship.

The ministry of generous giving supplies needs and causes thanksgiving to overflow toward God. Paul says this generosity becomes evidence connected with their confession of the Gospel of Christ, and he finally erupts:
“Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”
There it is.
Behind every truly Christian gift stands a greater Gift.
Jesus.
We give because God first gave.
We love because we have been loved.
We open our hands because Christ opened His arms on a cross.
We stop clutching temporary treasures because an eternal treasure has taken hold of us.
Maybe you cannot give ten percent right now.
Maybe you are drowning in debt.
Maybe you are buying groceries with trembling hands.
Maybe you are supporting elderly parents.
Maybe medical bills have swallowed what little margin you once had.
Do not let another human being weaponize Scripture to manufacture shame where Scripture gives room for willing, proportionate generosity.
God sees the heart.
And remember the widow Jesus watched giving two small coins.
Human beings saw an insignificant amount.
Jesus saw sacrifice.
But perhaps your situation is different.
Perhaps you could give far more than ten percent and barely notice.
Perhaps God has prospered you, but your lifestyle expanded every time your income did.
A larger house.
Another upgrade.
Another gadget.
Another vacation.
Another package arriving at the door.
And somewhere between “God blessed me” and “I deserve this,” generosity became whatever was left over.
Then maybe the question “Do Christians have to tithe?” is protecting you from the question your heart does not want to hear:
How much is enough for me?
There are believers for whom ten percent would be an enormous act of faith.
There are others for whom ten percent may be remarkably easy.
The New Testament does not lower the vision of generosity.
It takes the ruler away and aims at the heart.
Give deliberately.
Give willingly.
Give proportionately.
Give generously.
Give sacrificially when God leads.
Support faithful Gospel ministry.
Care for people in need.
Provide for your responsibilities.
Do not give because someone frightened you.
Do not give because someone promised that God would make you rich.
Do not give because you think money can purchase divine favor.
You cannot buy what Jesus purchased with blood.
Give because Christ is worthy.
And if ten percent helps you begin living generously, begin there.
If you can joyfully do more, do not let ten percent become the ceiling of your obedience.
And if you genuinely cannot reach that number, do not pretend before God. Begin faithfully with what you can give, ask Him for wisdom, order your finances carefully, and grow in generosity.
But whatever the percentage…
do not give God leftovers.
Give Him your heart.
And now I need to say something important about Gospel Warrior itself.
If these articles have helped you return to Scripture…
if something here has confronted sin without hiding grace…
if these messages have reached you at two in the morning when nobody knew you were struggling…
if they have helped you remember that Jesus has not finished writing your story…
then you can help this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces your responsibility to your local church, your family, believers in need, or wherever else God is calling you to give.
It does not.
But voluntary support of Gospel work is thoroughly consistent with the New Testament vision of believers using their resources to serve Christ, meet needs, and advance faithful ministry.
But please hear this clearly.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot purchase salvation.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Christ already paid the price we could never pay.
And money is not the only way you can help.
That costs nothing.
One share could place this message in front of them tonight.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is nothing more than rules.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions nobody in church ever allowed them to ask.
And I want you to do something even more important than sharing.
Has giving been worship for you…
or has it been guilt?
Have you used “grace” as an excuse to keep everything for yourself?
Have you been afraid that God would punish you financially if you missed ten percent?
Has money quietly become the part of your life you do not want Jesus touching?
No pretending.
No performance.
There may be someone reading your comment who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps this is the scandal underneath the entire question.
We keep asking how much we owe God.
Ten percent?
Five?
Twenty?
But the Gospel announces something far more astonishing.
You owed a debt you could never repay.
And instead of demanding payment from your empty hands…
God gave.
Christ came.
Christ obeyed.
Christ suffered.
Christ was crucified.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And sinners who bring nothing but repentance and faith receive forgiveness they could never afford.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that does not merely change where you go when you die.
Grace changes what you live for while you are still breathing.
Including what you do with money.
So should Christians tithe ten percent?

Christians are not given a simple New Testament command imposing ten percent on every believer in the same covenantal form in which Israel received its tithing laws. Yet Christians are unmistakably called to something that can be even more searching: intentional, willing, proportionate, cheerful, generous, sometimes deeply sacrificial stewardship under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Ten percent can be a wise beginning.
It should never become an excuse to tell Jesus:
“The rest is mine.”
Because maybe the most important number in Christian giving was never ten.
Maybe it was one hundred.
Not necessarily one hundred percent placed in an offering.
But one hundred percent surrendered to the ownership of Christ.
Your spending surrendered.
Your saving surrendered.
Your giving surrendered.
Your earning surrendered.
Your plans surrendered.
Your future surrendered.
Your heart surrendered.
All of it placed beneath the pierced hands of the One who gave everything to redeem you.
And perhaps when we finally understand that…
we stop asking:
“Jesus, how much do I have to give You?”
And begin asking:
“Jesus, everything I have came from You. How do You want me to use it?”
That question cannot be answered by a calculator.
It can only be answered by a surrendered heart.
The Gospel never asks you to purchase grace. It reveals a Savior whose grace was so costly that, once you truly see Him, clenched hands begin to open.
